analysis.one_liner: Massive federal investment in affordable housing: housing vouchers for all who qualify, plus billions for homeless programs.
analysis.headline: The Housing for All Act never got a hearing or vote in any of its four House committees before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would authorize roughly $125 billion in new federal spending on affordable housing over the coming years: $45 billion a year for the Housing Trust Fund, $40 billion for HOME block grants, hundreds of thousands of new housing choice vouchers, and large sums for homelessness services, legal help against evictions, and converting hotels and motels into housing.
analysis.who_benefits: Extremely low-income renters and people experiencing homelessness or at risk of it: the bill would expand vouchers to households earning up to half of the extremely-low-income limit, fund permanent supportive housing for the elderly and people with disabilities, pay for free legal help for tenants facing eviction, and support programs like safe parking lots for people living in vehicles.

how_it_helps.text: Expands housing choice vouchers, which pay part of rent for low-income households, to more eligible families and makes the assistance an entitlement — meaning any qualifying household would get one rather than joining a years-long waitlist [S3][S2].

Authorizes $45 billion per year for the Housing Trust Fund, the main federal fund for building and preserving affordable housing, which currently relies on profits from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac [S2][S3].
Creates grants for free legal assistance to low-income tenants facing eviction ($800 million) and for converting hotels, motels, and malls into permanent housing ($500 million) [S3].

Funds homelessness programs at scale: $15 billion for the Continuum of Care program (at least half for permanent housing for people with disabilities), $5 billion for Emergency Solutions Grants, and $2.5 billion for supportive housing for the elderly [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through roughly $125 billion in new authorizations over ten years; landlords and property owners could also face more competition for tenants with stronger legal representation, and more federal housing money raises demand for scarce housing in tight markets.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes very large sums (about $125 billion over ten years, including $45 billion a year for the Housing Trust Fund) without specifying a tax offset or how the spending would be paid for [S3].

Vouchers pay landlords market rents; pouring new federal money into housing demand without new supply can push rents up further in tight markets, an objection housing economists raise to voucher expansion alone [S3 — bill addresses supply only via the Housing Trust Fund and HOME].
Critics of a voucher entitlement note that making aid automatic removes cost control flexibility and makes future spending open-ended once eligibility is locked in [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are direct and large for the people hit hardest by the housing crisis — the roughly 600,000 Americans who are homeless and the millions of extremely low-income renters paying more than half their income in rent — while the costs are diffuse, spread across federal taxpayers. The strongest honest objection is design, not purpose: much of the bill expands demand for housing (vouchers) more than supply (only the Trust Fund and HOME money build units), so in tight markets some of the money could end up flowing to landlords through higher rents rather than to tenants through lower ones.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees when it was introduced in March 2022, then to subcommittees; none of them acted on it, and no floor vote ever happened before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the bill on March 8, 2022 with 17 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support [S1][S4].

It was referred to four committees at once — Financial Services, Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, and Transportation and Infrastructure — a common way for a bill to die, since every committee with a claim on it must act before the bill can move [S5].

Over the following eight months it was sent only to subcommittees (Health in March 2022; Highways and Transit in March 2022; Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties in November 2022); no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded [S5].
The bill never received a floor vote in the House and never came up in the Senate before the 117th Congress expired on January 3, 2023 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who are homeless or at risk of eviction did not gain, since the bill died without a vote; no committee ever scheduled it, so no legislator or bloc had to go on record against it. Homeless services providers and affordable housing developers did not get the new funding streams the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody gained; the bill died without a vote

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Housing for All Act of 2022 in the House on March 8, 2022.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.

against.name: House Financial Services, Judiciary, Energy and Commerce, and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral but never scheduled a hearing or markup in the ten months before Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Under the rules, a bill with no Republican support and no committee action requires the majority to schedule it; the House majority never brought the bill to the floor.

against.name: Senate
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill; no companion Senate version is recorded.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had 17 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican ones — a one-party bill that was never scheduled for committee action or a floor vote.

industries.note: A voucher entitlement plus free legal help for tenants facing eviction would guarantee rent payments through vouchers (a benefit to landlords) but would also mean tenants represented by lawyers in eviction cases, making evictions slower and costlier. The bill would tighten the balance between landlords and tenants.

industries.industry: Homeless services providers and housing developers
industries.note: Billions in new grant funding for continuum of care, emergency solutions, hotel/motel conversions, safe parking, and mobile crisis teams would flow to these organizations, which already deliver services for people experiencing homelessness.

By authorizing appropriations directly to the Housing Trust Fund, the bill would reduce reliance on the mortgage giants' earnings as the fund's sole source, loosening the link between mortgage-market profits and affordable housing money.
